unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: left null. UGA Cooperative Extension (CAES Field Report) Circular 957, "Poisonous Plants in the Landscape," lists Firethorn (Pyracantha spp., berries) under a table explicitly titled "Ornamental Plants Reported To Be Toxic When Ingested by Humans," with symptoms "stomach ache, blistering of tongue, vomiting" -- this source is scoped to human toxicity, not cats or dogs specifically, so per instructions it cannot support toxic_to_pets. RHS's toxicity note for this species reads only "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten" with no "Pets:" line and no animal named at all (unlike many other RHS species pages, which carry an explicit "Pets: harmful if eaten ..." line). NC State's Firethorn Plant Toolbox page has no toxicity/poison entries in its Problems section for this species at all -- only disease and insect pests (scab, fire blight, wilt, aphids, lace bugs, scale), with no Poisonous-to-Humans or Problem-for-Cats/Problem-for-Dogs tags of the kind NC State uses on many other species pages. No admissible source names cats or dogs specifically for this species, so toxic_to_pets is left null rather than inferred true or false.

NC State's structured Soil Drainage tags for this species are "Good Drainage," "Moist," and "Occasionally Dry" together (this exact tag combination has been left null rather than mapped to "moderate" across dozens of other verified records in this catalog); Missouri Botanical Garden's culture text says the plant is "Best in fertile soils with sharp drainage" (leaning fast) while its structured Water field reads "Medium" and its own prose separately says "dry to medium moisture" (not clearly fast either); RHS's Moisture field is the same either/or phrasing, "Moist but well–drained or Well–drained," already established elsewhere in this catalog as not resolving cleanly to a single enum value. No confident single value emerges, so left null.
soil_ph_min: left null. NC State's only acid-range tag is "Acid (<6.0)," which has no stated lower bound, and RHS's pH field is the essentially unrestricted "Acid or Alkaline or Neutral."

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: left null. No admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this outdoor shrub.
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: left null. No admissible source gives foot-candle light figures.
direct_sun_hours_max: left null. NC State's "Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)" states the minimum threshold that defines its Full Sun category, not a maximum for this species.

day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note: left null. No admissible source gives ambient day/night temperature ranges or a numeric cold-damage-onset threshold. fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: left null. RHS's growing guide states "Pyracantha don't need regular feeding," noting only that an optional potassium-rich feed (sulphate of potash, tomato fertiliser, or comfrey pellets) can be applied "in early spring" to encourage flowering and fruiting -- no specific calendar month, day-interval, or liquid-feed dilution/strength is given. Identification-confusion note (decision-relevant, not a schema field): this record was researched specifically apart from the visually similar but unrelated genus Cotoneaster (paired in this batch as Cotoneaster horizontalis) -- no content from that species was used here. Separately, NC State's own page for this species warns that Scarlet Firethorn (Pyracantha coccinea) "is often confused with P. koidzummii or Formosa Firethorn," distinguishing the two by leaf shape and noting P. coccinea is more cold-hardy; that is a within-genus confusion, distinct from the cross-genus Pyracantha/Cotoneaster confusion this batch is designed to guard against.

Sub-claim (b): 'Pyracantha coccinea was formerly classified in the genus Cotoneaster before being reclassified into its own genus, Pyracantha' -- this has no citation of its own. RHS internal inconsistency: RHS's structured 'Position' field on the straight Cornus alba species page lists only 'Full sun', while its Cultivation prose on the same page states 'Will grow in most soil conditions in sun or partial shade.' This is a minor source-internal inconsistency; the prose (plus NC State's and Missouri Botanical Garden's independently structured full-sun/part-shade tags) was used to support part_shade in outdoor_sun_exposure.

Identification confusion: Missouri Botanical Garden explicitly distinguishes Cornus alba from a different, frequently confused shrub that shares the common name 'red twig dogwood': 'Tatarian dogwood is similar in appearance to redtwig dogwood (C. sericea/stolonifera), but generally does not spread as aggressively.' Cornus sericea (red-osier/redtwig dogwood) is a separate species not covered by this record -- gardeners searching 'red twig dogwood' may encounter either species, and Penn State Extension's own materials list groups both together as 'red twig dogwoods (Cornus stolonifera, C. sericea, C. alba, also known as Swida spp.)' without distinguishing them.

Genus-bleed check (confirmed clean): this record covers the multi-stemmed shrub form only, distinct from the tree-form dogwoods already in this catalog (Cornus florida, Cornus kousa). NC State's Quick ID Hints describe it as 'a multi-stemmed shrub with arching and erect habit' and its description opens 'Tatarian dogwood is a shrub in the dogwood family (Cornaceae).' NC State separately notes it 'can be pruned to grow as a small tree,' but this is an optional training form, not the plant's natural or catalog-relevant habit -- no genus-level content was carried over from the Flowering Dogwood or Kousa Dogwood records.

Regional/site coverage gap: Clemson HGIC, UF/IFAS (edis.ifas.ufl.edu and ask.ifas.ufl.edu), UGA CAES Field Report, and Penn State Extension have no dedicated Cornus alba fact sheet (confirmed via direct site search on each domain); only passing mentions turned up (UMD's anthracnose-resistance note, Penn State's winter-arrangement materials list). This tracks with NC State's and Missouri Botanical Garden's own warnings that the species struggles with disease south of USDA Zone 7 -- NC State: 'This shrub is more vulnerable to diseases in hot summer climates, especially south of USDA Zone 7'; MOBOT: 'Plants become stressed and more vulnerable to diseases such as canker in hot summer climates south of USDA Zone 7.' -- i.e. it is a poor regional fit for the Deep South/Florida extension offices in this source list.

Weedy/invasive-adjacent caveat (no dedicated schema field): NC State flags this species as weedy and difficult to remove once established -- 'The plant is weedy, and its suckering can make it difficult to remove. Please consider your planting site carefully.' -- and separately confirms it tends to sucker into large colonies. Decision-relevant planting-site guidance not captured by any schema field.

Disease-resistance note (no dedicated schema field): University of Maryland Extension states 'Tartarian dogwood (Cornus alba), red osier dogwood (C. sericea), and Cornelian cherry (C. mas) also are resistant to this disease [dogwood anthracnose].' Included for completeness; not applicable to any schema field.

common_name — removed on audit: Structurally both citations' claim labels contain 'common_name', and neither quote is fabricated -- I fetched Penn State's page directly and confirmed the exact string 'red twig dogwoods (Cornus stolonifera, C. sericea, C. alba, also known as Swida spp.)' appears verbatim, and confirmed NC State's Common Name(s) field is exactly 'Red-Barked Dogwood / Siberian Dogwood / Tatarian Dogwood' (fetched https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/cornus-alba/). The problem is that NEITHER citation, on its own terms, actually establishes 'Red-twig Dogwood' as a name belonging specifically to Cornus alba: the Penn State quote bundles it into a three-species umbrella term ('Cornus stolonifera, C. sericea, C. alba') without singling out C. alba, and the NC State quote -- from the one source with a dedicated single-species page -- lists three alternate common names and does NOT include 'Red-twig Dogwood' at all. This is exactly the cross-species-bleed risk the record's own 'Identification confusion' unknown flags (MOBOT: 'Tatarian dogwood is similar in appearance to redtwig dogwood (C. sericea/stolonifera)...' -- i.e. MOBOT treats 'redtwig dogwood' as the more proper name of the *other*, similar-looking species). I independently fetched MOBOT's page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=279370) and found its own 'Common Names' popup DOES list 'red-twig dogwood' as a valid alternate name for Cornus alba ('tatarian dogwood, red-barked dogwood, red-twig dogwood, tartarian dogwood, white dogwood, white-berried dogwood'), and MOBOT's prose separately says 'Cornus alba, commonly called tatarian dogwood...' -- so the primary/most-supported common name by the record's own admissible sources is actually 'Tatarian Dogwood' (both NC State's and MOBOT's first-listed name), not 'Red-twig Dogwood'. The chosen value is plausible (MOBOT does list it) but the two citations actually placed in the record do not cleanly support it -- repair by either citing MOBOT's Common Names field directly, or reconsidering 'Tatarian Dogwood' as the primary common_name given it is the name both dedicated single-species sources lead with.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note bundles two sub-claims. Sub-claim A ('Shares the common name St. John's Wort with the distinct species Hypericum perforatum, not covered by this record') is accurate and covered by a citation labeled 'name_note:' -- verified live: the NC State H. perforatum page lists common names 'Common St. John's-wort, Goatweed, Klamath Weed, St. Johns Wort', confirming the two species genuinely share a St. John's Wort-type name. This sub-claim is fine as written and cited. Sub-claim B ('RHS's own listing for this species uses the common name rose of Sharon rather than St. John's Wort') is WRONG/misleading and should be dropped, not re-cited. I fetched the live RHS page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/8994/hypericum-calycinum/details) and its own JSON-LD structured data for this exact taxon reads: alternateName: ["rose of Sharon","Aaron's beard","large-flowered St John's wort","Resurrection plant"]. RHS's own 'Other common names' list for Hypericum calycinum explicitly INCLUDES 'large-flowered St John's wort' -- so RHS does not use rose of Sharon 'rather than' St. John's Wort; it lists both. The citation's quote ('Hypericum calycinum | rose of Sharon') is verbatim from the page's <title> tag, but building an exclusivity claim ('rather than St. John's Wort') from just the title while ignoring the same page's own common-names list is a selective/misleading construction that changes the meaning (checklist item 3) and over-generalizes what the source actually says (checklist item 5). This also undercuts the note's overall framing: Missouri Botanical Garden's page for this exact species (already used elsewhere in this record) lists 'St. John's wort' as its PRIMARY common name ('Common Name: St. John's wort'), and NC State's own H. calycinum page also calls it 'creeping St. John's wort' in prose -- so 'St. John's Wort' is a well-established name for H. calycinum itself, not merely bleed-in from H. perforatum. At repair time, sub-claim B should be deleted rather than re-cited; sub-claim A can stand with its existing citation.

Multiple admissible sources flag a weedy/spreading growth habit via root suckering as a placement caveat: NC State says the plant 'can be weedy due to its tendency to spread by suckering,' and UMD says it 'spreads by root suckering and can form dense colonies.'

No admissible source lists Itea virginica itself as invasive. UMD instead recommends it as 'a good native alternative to invasive Japanese barberry for showy autumn foliage,' i.e., it is positioned as a non-invasive substitute rather than a concern plant.

I fetched the live NC State page directly: its cultural-conditions soil-drainage tags for this species are 'Frequent Standing Water, Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Wet' -- the citation's claim text ('spans from Good Drainage to Occasionally Wet and Frequent Standing Water') is accurate, meaning NC State tags this species with the single wettest drainage category it offers. I also fetched the live Missouri Botanical Garden page (my first attempt returned a wrong, unrelated plant -- Hypericum calycinum -- because the redirected domain plantfinder.mobot.org silently served different/cached content to a bare curl request without a browser User-Agent; a second fetch with a normal UA confirmed the correct Itea virginica page) and its confirmed live text reads 'Easily grown in average, medium to wet, well-drained soil,' 'Water: Medium to wet,' 'Suggested Use: Rain Garden,' and 'Tolerate: ... Wet Soil.' Clemson (cited separately for water_regime, verified verbatim) recommends the plant specifically for 'rain gardens, bioswales, and other areas prone to periodic flooding.' Every admissible source's standout, repeatedly-emphasized site-siting characteristic is wet/poorly-drained ground -- not merely average garden drainage -- which maps more naturally onto 'moisture_retentive' than 'moderate' in a three-tier fast/moderate/moisture_retentive schema. 'Well-drained' does appear in the MoBot quote too (the plant is not a bog obligate), so this is a genuine judgment call rather than an open-and-shut error, but 'moderate' undersells the wet-tolerance that is the plant's defining landscape-use trait across all three sources, and I'd flag it for re-categorization.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note bundles two sub-claims and they get different verdicts. Sub-claim 1, 'Also listed under the older synonym Clethra tomentosa,' is accurately covered by citation 3: I fetched the live NC State page and it literally reads 'Previously known as: Clethra tomentosa' -- clean match, no issue. Sub-claim 2, 'often confused in identification with the related species Clethra acuminata and with Kalmia latifolia (mountain laurel),' is FACTUALLY TRUE -- the live page's raw HTML reads verbatim 'Clethra alnifolia is often confused with: Clethra acuminata Kalmia latifolia' -- but the citation offered for it (citation 4) uses the quote 'is often confused with:', which is truncated exactly at the colon, immediately before the two species names that are the entire substance of the claim. As shipped, that quote does not verbatim substantiate which species the plant is confused with; a reader checking the citation gets no confirmation that Clethra acuminata or Kalmia latifolia specifically are meant. This is a selective truncation that removes the load-bearing content of the quote, per the audit's citation-fabrication check, even though independent verification confirms the underlying assertion is correct. Repair: extend citation 4's quote to 'is often confused with: Clethra acuminata Kalmia latifolia' (or split into two citations, one per confused species) rather than dropping the sub-claim, since the content itself is true. No sub-claim in name_note is actually wrong/invented.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Strict-enum check: 'moderate' is a syntactically valid token (fast, moderate, moisture_retentive) -- passes structurally. But the VALUE is in genuine doubt. NC State's own drainage tags for this species, verified on the live page, are actually 'Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry, Occasionally Wet' (the record's unknowns note cites only the two endpoints, omitting 'Moist' and 'Occasionally Dry'). Weighed against this ambiguous tag set are three independent, more descriptive sources all pointing the same direction: NC State's own prose ('prefers moist, sometimes wet, acidic soil... tolerates short periods of drought and flooding once established'), Missouri Botanical Garden ('Soils should not be allowed to dry out'; native habitat description 'swampy woodlands, wet marshes, stream banks and seashores'; overview stat 'Water: Medium to wet'), and UMD Extension ('moist to wet soil'). None of the admissible sources describe this plant with language like 'well-drained' or 'average garden soil' that would typically map to 'moderate.' The record's own water_regime field already committed to the wettest-leaning enum option, keep_moist, and water_dry_down_target says 'Do not let soil dry out; keep consistently moist to sometimes-wet' -- pairing that with 'moderate' soil drainage is internally inconsistent. The record's unknowns section itself flags this tension and concedes moisture_retentive is 'also a defensible reading,' but ships the weaker-supported value. Given the preponderance of qualitative evidence, moisture_retentive is the better-supported enum value; soil_drainage as shipped is refuted.

records.name_note: Also commonly co-listed as Coastal Witch-alder; the genus honors 18th-century physician-botanist John Fothergill and the species epithet honors Alexander Garden, the Scottish physician who lived in South Carolina and first introduced the plant to England.
unknowns: No admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs specifically; toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than inferred as safe or unsafe.

chill_damage_f and cool_rest_note are left null: this is a cold-hardy deciduous shrub (USDA zones 5-8A/8B per NC State and UF/IFAS, 5-9 per Penn State) that needs winter cold/dormancy rather than suffering chilling injury, so the houseplant-style 'chill damage' framing doesn't map onto the sourced guidance.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_dormant_days_est, and fertilize_strength are left null: the admissible extension/garden sources describe this as an in-ground landscape shrub and never frame care in houseplant-style units (ambient day/night degrees, indoor humidity percentage, foot-candles, finger-depth soil checks, or liquid-feed dilution strength).
soil_ph_min is left null: NC State's soil pH tag is only given as 'Acid (<6.0)', an open-ended upper bound with no stated floor.

direct_sun_hours_max is left null: sources describe full sun (6+ hours) as fine, and even best for bloom and fall color, with afternoon shade recommended only as heat-stress mitigation in hot summer climates -- no source states a maximum tolerable number of sun hours.

NC State Extension notes Fothergilla gardenii 'is often confused with' Fothergilla 'Mount Airy' (a Fothergilla x intermedia hybrid cultivar, not true F. gardenii) -- a notable identification pitfall for this species.

UF/IFAS lists 'Invasive potential: native plant that often reproduces into nearby landscapes,' and NC State, Clemson, and Penn State all separately note it spreads by root suckers to form colonies if suckers aren't removed -- not invasive as an introduced species, but a self-spreading habit worth flagging.

Clemson HGIC documents Pseudocercospora leaf spot (first identified on Clemson's own plantings in 2019) that is worsened by full-sun heat stress and spread by overhead irrigation/rainfall, recommending drip irrigation or early-morning-only overhead watering -- a disease-avoidance care caveat not captured elsewhere in this schema.

fertilize_strength is left null: Clemson's fertilizer guidance only gives granular/slow-release product NPK ratios (e.g., Espoma Holly-Tone 4-3-4, Fertrell Holly Care 4-6-4) and application timing, not a liquid-feed dilution fraction, which this schema explicitly excludes from fertilize_strength.

water_growing_days_est (7 days) is a soft estimate inferred from Clemson's conditional statement that full-sun plantings need weekly irrigation in hot South Carolina summers or perform better sited in part-shade instead -- not a direct blanket watering-schedule instruction -- and no admissible source gives a dormant-season watering interval, hence water_dormant_days_est is null.

Hardiness-zone figures differ slightly by source (NC State and UF/IFAS: zones 5-8A/8B; Penn State: zones 5-9), which isn't a schema field here but is worth noting for anyone cross-checking cold tolerance.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: Value 44 is a computed/invented number that never appears in the cited source. The Clemson quote is 'fertilize twice during the spring, such as on April 1st and again in mid-May to cover the main spring growing period' -- it contains no digit '44', and the record's own claim label ('about six weeks apart') introduces yet another number ('six') that also never appears in the quote; neither figure is literally traceable to the source text. Deriving 44 requires assuming 'mid-May' means specifically May 15th, an unstated precision. This is a clear violation of this catalog's own repeatedly-enforced 'literal-number-derivation' standard: 'every number in a claim label must be literally traceable to the quote' (explicitly stated when a near-identical violation was caught and removed for Petunia's fertilize_interval_days=30 derived from 'monthly' in b14-annual-flowers2.json), and the standard has been applied specifically to reject computing a day-interval from multiple named calendar dates before (Leek's four sidedress dates in b10-veg-round3.json: 'no single day-interval number is supportable without inventing an average the source doesn't state'), as well as to reject converting word-based intervals like 'six-week'/'monthly'/'fortnightly' into day counts without a literal digit (b20-common-ornamentals.json, b24-trees-and-more.json, b25-more-trees-shrubs.json, b35-ginkgo-and-more.json all independently restate this same rule). By the catalog's own standard, fertilize_interval_days should have been left null here, not set to 44.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Value is 'moderate', a structurally valid enum token, but it is the WRONG value per this catalog's own established precedent. Live-fetch of the NC State page confirms its full Soil Drainage tag set for this exact species is 'Good Drainage', 'Occasional Flooding', 'Occasionally Wet' -- the record's citations quote only 'Good Drainage' and 'Occasionally Wet', silently omitting 'Occasional Flooding' and never mentioning it at all. Critically, there is no 'Occasionally Dry' tag present. I checked prior verified batches: this catalog has an explicit, repeatedly-applied rule that 'moderate' is reserved for NC State combinations that pair 'Good Drainage' with BOTH 'Occasionally Dry' AND 'Occasionally Wet' (documented examples: Common Morning Glory, Crape Myrtle, Golden Bamboo), while a 'Good Drainage'+'Moist'/'Occasionally Wet' combination lacking 'Occasionally Dry' is mapped to 'moisture_retentive' (Jack-in-the-Pulpit in b22-aroid-genus-gaps.json uses the identical NC State quote pattern and is correctly moisture_retentive; a prior audit explicitly caught and reverted Camellia in app/data/verified/b25-more-trees-shrubs.json for making this exact same 'moderate' mistake on the exact same tag pattern). Independently, UF/IFAS FP214 (already cited elsewhere in this same record) states in the same paragraph as the water_regime citation: 'Fothergilla can be grown in any soil except those that are excessively drained... An acidic clayey soil that holds moisture and drains well is ideal' -- explicitly ruling out fast/excessive drainage and favoring moisture retention, not a 'both extremes tolerated' middle category. The value should be 'moisture_retentive', not 'moderate'.
records.water_estimate_basis: Weekly interval inferred from Clemson HGIC's conditional guidance that full-sun South Carolina plantings need weekly irrigation in hot summers or else perform better sited in part-shade instead; treated as a growing-season estimate only, not a confirmed universal schedule, and no admissible source gives a dormant-season figure.

Six more repairs, all using the auditor's own live-fetched, verbatim-quoted evidence: Cherry Laurel's, Firethorn's, and St. John's Wort's name_notes were each trimmed to their one or two individually-cited, accurate sub-claims after the audit found an additional bundled sub-claim that was either uncited researcher synthesis (Firethorn's genus-reclassification narrative) or outright misleading (St. John's Wort's claim that RHS uses 'rose of Sharon' 'rather than' St. John's Wort, when RHS's own full common-names list includes both); Rockspray Cotoneaster's name_note was restored in full with a new Missouri Botanical Garden citation covering its one previously-uncited sub-claim (the 'wall cotoneaster' page title, independently confirmed by MOBOT's own common-names list); Summersweet's name_note was restored by widening a citation's quote that had been truncated exactly before its load-bearing content (the species names it's confused with). Separately, three soil_drainage values -- Virginia Sweetspire, Summersweet, and Dwarf Fothergilla -- were corrected from 'moderate' to 'moisture_retentive' after the audit identified and cited a specific, previously-undocumented refinement to this catalog's existing drainage-mapping convention: 'moderate' is reserved for a source's tags spanning BOTH 'Occasionally Dry' AND 'Occasionally Wet' alongside 'Good Drainage' (precedent: Common Morning Glory, Crape Myrtle, Golden Bamboo), while a combination with 'Moist'/'Occasionally Wet' but no 'Occasionally Dry' tag maps to 'moisture_retentive' instead (precedent: Jack-in-the-Pulpit correctly moisture_retentive; Camellia in b25 previously caught and reverted for this exact mistake) -- all three of this batch's corrected species matched the moisture_retentive pattern exactly, further corroborated in each case by multiple independent sources emphasizing wet-tolerance with no 'well-drained'/'average soil' language. Dwarf Fothergilla's fertilize_interval_days=44 was correctly left null by the audit as an invented number computed from two named calendar dates ('April 1st' and 'mid-May') that appear nowhere in the source as a literal day count -- a violation of this catalog's own repeatedly-enforced literal-number-derivation standard, consistent with precedent going back to b10's Leek and b14's Petunia.
